1. Understand: the motor is fixed, an AeroTech K805 the builder already owns. Apogee at least 2,000 m (minimum) and the request asks for the highest stable flight, so overshoot is wanted. Landing under 6 m/s (maximum). Body tube 70 mm or less (maximum). Wind about 4 m/s (given). Rail and site unstated, so the 1.5 m rail and sea level, and I will say so.
2. Feasibility: 2,000 m in vacuum needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 2000) = 198 m/s at burnout, and drag wants 300 m/s or better. A 70 mm ceiling also forces the mount to be inside a tube that is only just wider than a 54 mm case, so the airframe is nearly minimum diameter and that helps.

Design request. Fresh L1 here. Got a spare Cesaroni I216. What's the highest stable rocket I can build for it? It has to land under 5.5 m/s. Winds are typically 10 mph. The rail is 6 ft long. Please provide the full design.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: motor fixed, a Cesaroni I216, from a Level 1 flyer. The goal is the highest stable rocket for that motor, so overshoot is wanted. Landing under 5.5 m/s (maximum). Wind about 10 mph = 4.4 m/s (given). Rail 6 ft = 1.83 m (given, longer than the 1.5 m default, so it goes into every call). Site altitude and payload unstated, so sea level and nothing carried.
2. Feasibility: an I is 320 to 640 N*s, so a 38 mm I in a rocket that stays close to motor diameter is a 2 to 4 km proposition depending on drag. The 5.5 m/s landing limit with a light airframe is easy with a metre-class canopy, but from several kilometres a single large canopy makes a very long descent, so a small drogue plus a main at low altitude is the practical answer. I need the motor numbers first.

Looking for help with a build. From 3,500 m, under 30 s total flight, landing under 15 ft/s. Plan for 2 m/s wind. What would you build?

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: no motor given, so I choose. Requirements: apogee 3,500 m, total flight time under 30 s (maximum), landing under 15 ft/s = 4.6 m/s (maximum), wind 2 m/s (given). Rail 1.5 m, sea level, nothing carried.
2. Feasibility: I should check whether these requirements can coexist before designing. Covering 3,500 m in under 30 s means a mean descent of 3500 / 30 = 117 m/s, but landing under 4.6 m/s means the final descent must be that slow, and a parachute descent from even the last 300 m at 4.6 m/s takes 300 / 4.6 = 65 s on its own. So the 30 s limit cannot be met by any design that also meets the landing limit, and I will say so plainly rather than invent a number. That leaves the altitude as the requirement I can actually work on: 3,500 m needs roughly 700 N*s per kilogram of liftoff mass, which points at a 54 mm K-class reload in a 60 mm minimum-diameter airframe, and I want the highest impulse that case will take.
3. Size: 60.3 mm fiberglass airframe with a 1.2 mm wall, leaving a 57.3 mm mount around the 54 mm case, which is as narrow as a 54 mm motor allows. Estimated liftoff mass about 2.6 kg with a reload of that class aboard. Thrust-to-weight for a high-thrust K is well above 3, and rail exit follows from the high acceleration over a 1.5 m rail. Recovery needs to land at 4.6 m/s against roughly 1.0 kg of dry structure, which at 4.0 m/s needs 2 * 1.0 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4^2) = 1.25 m^2, a diameter of sqrt(4 * 1.25 / 3.1416) = 1.26 m, so a 1.6 m main at 300 m with a 0.5 m drogue.
4. Draft: 60.3 mm airframe 1.10 m of tube, 0.30 m haack nose, four basswood fins with a 0.12 m span, a 57.3 mm mount long enough for a 54 mm K case, apogee drogue and 1.6 m main, in 2 m/s wind. I am looking up the highest-impulse 54 mm K I can find to fill it.

Hey! I'm Level 1. My club gave me an I216. Design around it. Stable, as much altitude as is reasonable, landing under 5 m/s. Keep it single-stage. We launch off a 1 m rod. Thanks!

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: single stage (fixed). Motor fixed to a Cesaroni I216 (fixed). Apogee "as much as is reasonable" with no number, so I maximise altitude subject to every safety gate and a sane build. Landing speed under 5 m/s (maximum, stricter than the usual 6). Launch rod 1 m (fixed, and short, so rail-exit speed is the gate I must watch). Wind and launch angle are not stated, so I assume 2 m/s and a vertical launch.
2. Feasibility: clean burnout speed for a couple of kilometres is 200 m/s or more, and past Mach 1 the airframe keeps only a fraction of its ideal height, so 350 to 400 m/s of burnout is the real ask. On an I at 320 to 640 N*s that means staying near or below about 1.6 kg at liftoff. The 1 m rod is the sharper constraint: with a heavy I-motor rocket the net acceleration will be around 190 m/s^2, so the exit speed is only about sqrt(2 * 190 * 1) = 19.5 m/s, above the 15 m/s floor but with little margin, and losing mass is what protects it. I need the motor's exact impulse, case size, mass and delays before sizing the hull.

The motor sold as I800 is 419I800-15A, 38 mm, 415.5 N*s and 0.8023 kN of average thrust over half a second. I600R is filed as class J at 640.1 N*s, so it is not an L1 motor at all and I must not use it. So the verdict is that this request is infeasible, and the constraint that cannot be met is the L1 motor limit. Reaching 15,240 m needs something over 1,500 N*s by my step-2 arithmetic; an H or I motor cannot exceed 640 N*s, and the best one here gives 634.6, which is 1500/634.6 = 2.36 times too little. No airframe change closes a factor of 2.4 in impulse. What I can do is offer the closest honest version: a minimum-diameter 38 mm rocket on that 634I540-16A, built to go as high as an L1 motor sensibly allows, which is the real answer to the beginner's question and is a rocket that can actually be built.

Mass at phenolic 1350, glass 1850 kg/m^3: shell pi*(0.021^2 - 0.0195^2) = 0.000191 m^2, times 0.55 m is 0.000105 m^3 and 0.000105*1350 = 0.142 kg. Three fins with a 0.5*(0.10+0.05)*0.07 = 0.00525 m^2 face at 2.5 mm are 0.00525*0.0025 = 0.0000131 m^3 and 0.0000131*1850 = 0.0243 kg each, 0.073 kg the set. Gates: weight 0.94*9.81 = 9.22 N against 548 N is 548/9.22 = 59:1. Net acceleration (548 - 9.22)/0.94 = 573 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2*573*1.5) = 41.5 m/s. 2. Feasibility: coming under a ceiling is easier than reaching a floor, because two levers push down. Ballast is the lazy option, but on a light airframe it can do surprising things and it adds recoverable mass. Impulse is more predictable, since apogee tracks roughly with the square of it, and this mount is 38 mm so any H fits the same hardware with no new case. messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Competition rules for us: It needs to clear 350 m. It needs to come down at 15 ft/s or less. Room for a 75 g payload module, please. Please flag anything risky.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: three requirements. "Clear 350 m" is a minimum, so apogee must be at least 350 m with no upper bound, and I will aim a little above so build variance cannot drop it under. Landing is 15 ft/s or less, and 15*0.3048 = 4.57 m/s, which is a max and is tighter than the 6 m/s default. The payload is a fixed 75 g module, which has to ride as an actual mass in the airframe, not be assumed away. "Flag anything risky" is an instruction about the answer, so the final summary has to name the risks rather than only give a number. Not given: motor, rail, wind, recovery type, so I assume 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind and single deploy.

2. Feasibility: 350 m is easy on almost any mid-power motor, so the design is really driven by the two limits. The payload at 75 g is about 20 % of an estimated 380 g rocket and sits high, which is where stability comes from, so it helps rather than hurts. The landing limit of 4.57 m/s is the number that needs a real canopy: at roughly 0.45 kg that is about 0.43 m^2, so a 0.75 to 0.8 m chute. Nothing here looks infeasible; the risk is overshooting the altitude badly on too big a motor, which is not a failure but is wasteful. Looking up a couple of F motors so the altitude lands near 500 to 600 m rather than overshooting.

messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Competition rules for us: Needs to hit about 4,500 ft and come down within 2,000 ft of the pad in 5 mph wind. We want dual deploy on this one. We'd like the full design.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand:

Three flight numbers and one architecture requirement, in mixed units, so the conversions come first. 4,500 ft at 0.3048 m per ft is 1,371.6 m, target about 1,370 m. Within 2,000 ft of the pad is 609.6 m. 5 mph is 4.4704 m/s per mph, so 2.24 m/s of wind, and I fly the design in that wind. Dual deploy, meaning a drogue at apogee and a main lower down, is required rather than optional. Defaults where nothing was said: 1.5 m rail, landing under 6 m/s, site at sea level.

2. Feasibility:

The drift cap is what shapes the recovery. 610 m at 2.24 m/s allows 610/2.24 = 272 s of descent. On a single canopy falling at 5 m/s from 1,370 m the descent alone is 274 s, which already spends the whole budget before any ascent drift, so single deploy does not work here and the dual deploy requirement is not a preference, it is what makes the number reachable. Under a small drogue at roughly 15 m/s the 1,370 m down to 250 m leg takes about 75 s, and the last 250 m under a main at 4 m/s takes 63 s, so about 138 s and 310 m of drift, with room to spare.

Altitude is the second constraint. 1,370 m needs sqrt(2*9.81*1370) = 164 m/s of ballistic speed, so roughly 230 to 260 m/s at burnout against drag, which on a 0.6 kg airframe is H territory. I will size the fin area for margin rather than shave it. Looking up two 29 mm H motors and reading their thrust curves.

Both candidates are 29 mm and in the H class, so the airframe needs a 30.6 mm mount with a 0.8 mm wall to leave 29.0 mm of bore, inside a 38 mm body with a 1.5 mm wall and 35 mm of bore. Crossing the two motors: the AeroTech is 177.8 N*s at 152.6 N average and 190.5 N peak over 1.16 s at 0.2016 kg, and the Cesaroni is 206.2 N*s at 236.5 N average and 296.0 N peak over 0.87 s at 0.294 kg. Per kilogram of loaded motor the Cesaroni is worse, about 701 N*s/kg against about 882 N*s/kg for the AeroTech. It has the higher impulse and the higher peak, so I am building around it anyway and will read the altitude off the simulator rather than trusting a scaling law.

Mass: body shell pi*(0.019^2 - 0.0175^2) = 0.000172 m^2, times 0.80 m is 0.000138 m^3 and about 0.094 kg; nose 0.02 kg; fins 0.5*(0.10+0.04)*0.06 = 0.0042 m^2 of face, about 0.0044 kg each and 0.0132 kg for three; mount 0.0076 kg; centering rings 0.004 kg; drogue, main and their cords 0.05 kg; avionics bay 0.03 kg; and 0.09 kg of forward mass to pull the CG ahead of the fins. Dry 0.31 kg and about 0.61 kg on the pad loaded.

Gates: weight 0.61*9.81 = 5.99 N, so thrust-to-weight 236.5/5.99 = 39.5:1, and rail exit sqrt(2*((236.5 - 5.99)/0.61)*1.5) = 33.6 m/s.

Total about 360 m against the 610 m cap, and 3.1 m/s against the 6 m/s landing limit.

38 mm single stage, Cesaroni H with electronic deployment throughout since dual deploy needs an altimeter anyway, drogue at apogee and main at 250 m, fins sized large at a 0.10 m root and 0.06 m span to keep margin well above the gate. messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Goal is about 3,750 ft. With 15 mph wind it still has to land inside 2 miles of the pad. Single-chute recovery.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand:
- Target apogee: about 3750 ft, which is about 1140 m. Read "about" as within 5 percent, so the band is roughly 1090 m to 1200 m.
- Landing: within 2 miles of the pad, about 3.2 km. This is a maximum drift limit, so it is a hard max.
- Wind: 15 mph, about 6.7 m/s. I will pass this as the wind in every simulate call.
- Recovery: single chute, one deployment at apogee. The prompt does not ask for staging or clustering, so this is a single stage with one motor.
- Assumptions for the missing items: rail 1.5 m, launch angle 0 degrees, landing rate limit 6 m/s, because the prompt gives no landing speed limit.
- Fixed: single stage, single chute, 15 mph wind. Min: about 1090 m apogee. Max: about 1200 m apogee and about 3.2 km drift.

2. Feasibility:
- A 38 mm airframe with a loaded mass near 0.3 kg should reach this altitude with a single H-class motor. The I class has far more impulse and would overshoot by a wide margin.
- Candidates to look up: H128W (H class, 38 mm) and I200W (I class, 38 mm), so I can compare their impulse and delay before choosing.
- Rough check: a 0.3 kg rocket weighs about 3 N. A thrust-to-weight ratio of at least 5 is a safe launch target, and an H-class average thrust near 130 N would give a ratio far above that. I will confirm with the tool.
- The chute must hold the landing rate under 6 m/s with a 0.3 kg rocket. That needs a chute diameter near 0.3 m or more; I will check it in the simulation.
- Drift with 6.7 m/s wind over a descent of about 60 s is about 400 m, far below the 3.2 km limit. The wind is not the binding constraint.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee at most 2,000 ft = 610 m (a ceiling, so over is a failure). Motor diameter at most 38 mm (maximum). Total impulse at most 250 N*s (maximum). Wind about 10 mph = 4.5 m/s, so every flight carries that. Rail set at 3 degrees from vertical, so every flight carries that too. Recovery and landing limit are not stated: chute, at most 6 m/s touchdown.
2. Feasibility: 610 m with no drag needs sqrt(2*9.81*610) = 109 m/s at burnout, and a 38 mm motor of up to 250 N*s can deliver far more than that, so this is a ceiling problem like a field limit: the design has to be heavy enough that a legal H does not overshoot. The 3 degree rail tilt also costs height, since the flight spends its thrust off vertical. I want a 54 mm airframe around 1 kg and a modest H or a strong G; checking two motors to bracket the impulse.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee at least 1,500 ft = 457 m (minimum). Landing speed at most 5 m/s at touchdown (maximum, and stricter than the 6 m/s I would otherwise assume). Largest external body diameter at most 110 mm (maximum). Motor class, rail length and wind are not stated, so I assume the standard 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind and a vertical launch, and I stay with mid-power hardware. Single stage.
2. Feasibility: clean burnout speed for 457 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 457) = 94.7 m/s, and a wide airframe loses more to drag than a slim one, so 130 to 160 m/s of burnout is the real ask. I want a 54 mm body, comfortably under the 110 mm cap, which leaves room for a 29 mm mount, a chute and a harness. On a 0.36 kg rocket the 29 mm G motors give about 275 m/s of ideal velocity change, comfortably more than needed. I need impulse and delay options for the two I am considering.

Target 650 m, motor 29 mm or smaller, single-stage, wind ~15 km/h, site at 600 m elevation.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand:

Four conditions, and two of them are site conditions that change the answer if ignored. Target 650 m. Motor 29 mm or smaller, which caps the class in practice around G. Single stage. Wind about 15 km/h, which is 15/3.6 = 4.17 m/s, and the site is at 600 m elevation, which matters because air density at 600 m is about 7 % lower than sea level and that alone lifts every apogee. Defaults: 1.5 m rail, landing under 6 m/s.

I am reading the site elevation as a flight condition rather than a footnote, because at 600 m the rocket flies through thinner air both on the way up and on the way down, so it will go higher than the same design at sea level and will land faster, because thinner air gives less drag. The higher apogee changes the motor choice, and the faster landing works against the 6 m/s default; both have to be in the simulation.

2. Feasibility:

650 m needs sqrt(2*9.81*650) = 113 m/s of ballistic speed, so I estimate drag puts it nearer 140 m/s at burnout. A 29 mm case needs 29.0 mm of bore, so the mount is 30.6 mm outside and a 29 mm body cannot hold its own motor mount; the airframe has to be 38 mm outside, which is the diameter I will pay drag for. I guess that in a 38 mm airframe 650 m is a 0.3 to 0.5 kg rocket, which is small enough that an F or light G will do it without much ballast, and the question is which end of that range the drag pushes me to.

Two things to check with the tools rather than reason about: whether a light F overshoots in the thinner air at 600 m, and whether the wind at 4.17 m/s makes the single canopy drift unreasonable, since this brief does not give a landing area. Looking up an F and a G at 29 mm.

Three 18 mm casings are around 0.05 kg of that, which leaves under 0.1 kg of airframe, so this is a very light rocket and there is almost no room to be heavy.

Cluster geometry also constrains the diameter. Three 18 mm cases in a bundle need about 40 mm of inside diameter, which is a BT-60 at 41.6 mm; a 24.8 mm BT-50 will not take three mounts and a 33.4 mm BT-55 is marginal. So the airframe is 41.6 mm across, which is large frontal area for 7.5 N*s of impulse, and drag will be a big fraction of the flight. First real build here. We're an L3 team. I want to fly an AeroTech M1297. What's the highest stable rocket I can build for it? It has to land under 6 m/s. It should handle 10 mph wind. We launch off a 10 ft rail. Keep it simple if you can.

They want the highest altitude that stays stable, which I read as maximizing apogee while holding at least 1 cal of margin. Landing at most 6 m/s (maximum). Wind is 10 mph = 10 * 0.447 = 4.47 m/s (fixed). Rail is 10 ft = 10 * 0.3048 = 3.05 m (fixed). Angle and field elevation are not given, so a vertical sea-level launch. They asked to keep it simple, so one stage and one chute.
2. Feasibility: an M will go very high in a tube that barely clears the case. Stability is the constraint, because that motor is heavy and long. I need its impulse, diameter, mass and whether it has an ejection delay before I size the chute and the fins.

Hi, two-stage, an O booster and an M sustainer. I want it to hit about 10,000 m. Both stages need to land under 6 m/s. We launch off a 2.5 m rail. What would you build?

1. Understand: apogee about 10,000 m, within 5 percent, so 9,500 to 10,500 m. Two stages: an O-class booster below and an M-class sustainer above. Both stages land at under 6.0 m/s, which I apply to every section. Rail 2.5 m as stated, so pass rail_length_m 2.5. Wind not stated, so use the 2.0 m/s default and do not pass a wind value. Launch angle 0, site sea level by default.
2. Feasibility: 10,000 m is a high-power target. Ideal coast height from burnout speed v is v^2 / (2 * 9.81), so with no drag 10,000 m needs about 443 m/s at burnout, and drag takes a large share at high speed. The booster must carry the stack to a high speed, and the sustainer must add the rest. A two-stage with an O booster and an M sustainer is plausible on paper, but the result depends on drag, the stage masses and the stability, which only the simulator can settle. 4. Check: The simulator gives 2619.1 m. Against about 2,740 m that is (2740 - 2619.1) / 2740 = 4.4% low, inside the 5% band. Margin is 2.02 cal at rail exit and through the burn. Rail exit is 19.2 m/s, thrust-to-weight is 9.3, landing is 4.8 m/s under 6 m/s, and the chute opens at 19.3 s right at apogee. Liftoff mass is 2.13 kg, a bit over my 1.9 kg guess, which explains sitting low in the band. Peak Mach is 0.97, with no warning.

5. Fix: no change needed; altitude and the gates all pass.

6. Uncertainty: 2619.1 m is near the bottom of the 5% band, and the rocket came out heavier than I guessed. A lighter build will fly higher, a heavier one will drop out of the band. Rail exit is only 19.2 - 15 = 4.2 m/s above the gate, so the same extra mass would miss the rail before it missed the altitude by much. Chute Cd is 0.8 in the model. Drift is 812 m in a 2 m/s wind over a 531.9 s flight; nothing in the request limits that, but the recovery walk is long.
